Strike by Diversified Industrials Workers in Spain Halts Production Across Multiple Sites

MADRID, June 12 – Thousands of workers in Spain’s Diversified Industrials sector staged a coordinated walkout on Wednesday, bringing operations to a standstill at numerous plants and facilities across the country, union representatives and company officials said. The strike, which began at midnight, is the largest industrial action in the sector in more than a decade and has interrupted manufacturing processes, delayed shipments, and left factory floors idle.

Employees at several leading firms, including Grupo Rivas, Solventis Industrial, and Iberic Systems, joined the strike following the collapse of talks over wage increases and working conditions. The General Confederation of Industrial Workers (CGTI), the main union behind the action, said more than 80 percent of its 19,500 members in the sector had walked off the job. The union is demanding a 7 percent pay rise and improved overtime compensation.

“We have been in negotiations for months, but management has refused to meet our basic demands,” said CGTI spokesperson Marta Hernández at a rally outside the Grupo Rivas facility in Zaragoza. “Workers have made their contribution to the industry’s growth, and it is time for their sacrifices to be recognized.”

Grupo Rivas, one of Spain’s largest diversified industrial firms, suspended all shifts at its Madrid, Valencia, and Seville sites. Company spokesperson Luis Ortega said the company was “deeply concerned” about the impact of the stoppage and was assessing its ability to fulfill existing orders. “We respect our employees’ right to strike but urge a swift return to the negotiating table to resolve outstanding issues,” Ortega said.

Production lines at Solventis Industrial’s plants in Bilbao and Murcia were also idle, with management confirming that only a skeleton staff remained on site to ensure safety and equipment maintenance. At Iberic Systems, all assembly operations were halted, with company officials warning of mounting backlogs.

Analysts said the strike could have significant consequences for the sector if it continues into next week. “Diversified Industrials play a crucial role in Spain’s manufacturing base, and even a short disruption can have lingering effects on output and efficiency,” said Elena Ramos, senior analyst at Ibermonitor.

The Ministry of Industry has called on both sides to resume dialogue. “We urge social partners to seek an agreement that ensures the competitiveness of the sector while protecting workers’ rights,” a ministry statement said.

Union leaders indicated the strike would continue until further notice. “We are prepared to maintain this action as long as necessary,” Hernández said.
